title: Writing for Work & the Web
subtitle: Plan, write and structure clear content — from emails, proposals and instructions to web pages and docs.
outcomes: Plan any document around its reader and purpose
Write clear, concise words and sentences
Structure content with headings, lists, tables and paragraphs
Write emails, proposals and instructions, accessibly and for a global audience

toc.text: Use the acronym or the full term?
Distinguish active voice from passive voice in simple sentences
Distinguish active voice from passive voice in more complex sentences
Prefer active voice to passive voice
Focus each sentence on a single idea
Convert some long sentences to lists
Choose the correct type of list
Start numbered list items with imperative verbs
Focus each paragraph on a single topic
Don't make paragraphs too long or too short

lessons.title: Correspondence: Text Messages, Emails, Memos, and Letters
Correspondence: Text Messages, Emails, Memos, and Letters · Letters

toc.text: Proposals written as an assignment in a Technical Writing classes generally do the following:
The Life Cycle of a Project Idea
1. Do a careful audience and task analysis
3.  Determine the best approach to the step-by-step discussion
Some things to avoid where possible
Some techniques and approaches to consider
Use clear, concise, and unambiguous language
Use simpler words and shorter sentences
Use active voice and present tense
Use words in their primary sense
Use helper words and optional words
Address users and their needs directly
Use standard sentence structures and formatting

pool.q: Which kind of writing is primarily writer-centred?
pool.explain: They are written for the benefit of the writer; workplace writing should be reader-centred.
pool.evidence: Things like diaries and journals are primarily writer-centred, in that they are written for the benefit of the writer.

pool.q: What does reader-centred writing advise you to emphasise?
options: What you can do rather than what you can't
pool.explain: Focus on the positive.
pool.evidence: Focus on the positive: emphasize what you can do rather than what you can’t.

pool.q: Which question should you ask yourself before writing for a reader?
options: How long can I make this?
How many big words can I use?
Which font is the most decorative?
pool.explain: Audience analysis starts with knowing who will read it.
pool.evidence: Use these guidelines and ask yourself the following questions: Who is my target audience?

pool.q: What is the first step in designing any solution?
pool.explain: Design processes vary, but they start with the problem.
pool.evidence: One commonality you will likely find in examining other people’s design process diagrams is this: the first step in designing any solution is to clearly define the problem .

pool.q: What are many workplace communication tasks designed to do?
options: Solve a problem or improve a situation
pool.explain: That is why writing can follow a design process.
pool.evidence: In the workplace, many of the communications tasks you perform are designed to solve a problem or improve a situation.

pool.q: What question defines a "rhetorical situation"?
options: How many pages should it be?
Who is talking to whom about what, how, and why?
pool.explain: Its five components are purpose, writer, audience, message and context/culture.
pool.evidence: To define a “rhetorical situation,” ask yourself this question: “who is talking to whom about what, how, and why?”

pool.q: In the rhetorical situation, what does PURPOSE refer to?
pool.explain: Determining purpose is part of task analysis.
pool.evidence: PURPOSE refers to the why you are writing.

pool.q: What should you do if your document introduces many new terms?
options: Collect the definitions into a glossary
Use different words for each term each time
Put them all in the title
pool.explain: Define new terms, or link to existing explanations.
pool.evidence: If your document is introducing many terms, collect the definitions into a glossary.

pool.q: If a good explanation of an unfamiliar term already exists, what should you do?
options: Copy it word for word without credit
pool.explain: Don't reinvent the wheel.
pool.evidence: If the term already exists, link to a good existing explanation.

pool.q: Why does the lesson compare changing a term midway to renaming a variable in code?
options: Because writers should learn to code
Using terms consistently matters, just as code won't compile with inconsistent names
pool.explain: Use terms consistently.
pool.evidence: Use terms consistently If you change the name of a variable midway through a method, your code won’t compile.

pool.q: Which voice should the vast majority of sentences in technical writing use?
pool.explain: Active voice is usually clearer.
pool.evidence: The vast majority of sentences in technical writing should be in active voice.

pool.q: What is the formula of an active-voice sentence?
pool.explain: A passive sentence reverses the formula.
pool.evidence: Active Voice Sentence = actor + verb + target A passive voice sentence reverses the formula.

pool.q: According to many technical writers, what is the most important part of a sentence?
pool.explain: Pick the right verb and the rest will follow.
pool.evidence: Choose strong verbs Many technical writers believe that the verb is the most important part of a sentence.

pool.q: What is wrong with sentences that start with "There is" or "There are"?
options: They marry a generic noun to a generic verb
pool.explain: Often you can delete "There is" and use the true subject.
pool.evidence: Reduce there is / there are Sentences that start with There is or There are marry a generic noun to a generic verb.

pool.q: What do technical writers aim for, compared with comedy and horror writers?
pool.explain: Clarity is the technical writer's goal.
pool.evidence: Clear sentences Comedy writers seek the funniest results, horror writers strive for the scariest, and technical writers aim for the clearest.

pool.q: What makes a heading effective?
options: Concrete, descriptive language that tells the reader what to expect
pool.explain: Descriptive headings help readers navigate.
pool.evidence: Effective headings use concrete, descriptive language to tell the reader what to expect from the content of each section.

pool.q: What kind of headings should you avoid in technical reports?
options: "Function" headings that name a section's function instead of its content
pool.explain: Readers find content-describing headings more helpful.
pool.evidence: Avoid “function” headings when writing technical reports.

pool.q: When should you use a numbered list instead of a bulleted list?
options: Only for items with numbers in them
pool.explain: Rearranging a numbered list changes its meaning.
pool.evidence: Use a bulleted list for unordered items; use a numbered list for ordered items.

pool.q: What is an embedded (run-in) list?
options: A list inside a table cell
A list whose items are stuffed within a sentence
pool.explain: Long embedded lists are often clearer as bulleted or numbered lists.
pool.evidence: An embedded list (sometimes called a run-in list) contains items stuffed within a sentence.

pool.q: What happens if you rearrange the items in a bulleted list?
options: The list's meaning does not change
pool.explain: Bullets are for unordered items.
pool.evidence: In other words: If you rearrange the items in a bulleted list, the list's meaning does not change.

pool.q: Which is the most important sentence of any paragraph?
pool.explain: Busy readers focus on opening sentences.
pool.evidence: Write a great opening sentence The opening sentence is the most important sentence of any paragraph.

pool.q: What do good opening sentences establish?
options: A joke to warm up readers
pool.explain: Focus your writing energy on opening sentences.
pool.evidence: Good opening sentences establish the paragraph's central point.

pool.q: What is "netiquette"?
options: Proper etiquette for using the internet
pool.explain: Professional texting, email and social media require it.
pool.evidence: Text messaging, emailing, and posting on social media in a professional context requires that you be familiar with “netiquette,” or proper etiquette for using the internet.

pool.q: Why should a business email have a clear, brief, specific subject line?
options: It helps the recipient understand the essence of the message
It hides the email from spam filters
pool.explain: The subject line previews the message.
pool.evidence: Include a clear, brief, and specific subject line: this helps the recipient understand the essence of the message.

pool.q: What should your written business communication be?
options: Long, formal and full of jargon
As short as possible, even if unclear
pool.explain: It represents you and your company.
pool.evidence: your goal is to make it clear, concise, constructive, and professional.

pool.q: What are letters, in business communication?
options: Brief messages often sent to recipients outside the organisation
pool.explain: They are often on letterhead and limited to one or two pages.
pool.evidence: Letters are brief messages sent to recipients that are often outside the organization.

pool.q: What is a proposal, in the technical sense?
options: A summary of last year's sales
A document that tries to persuade the reader to implement a plan or approve a project
pool.explain: Proposals are persuasive documents.
pool.evidence: A proposal, in the technical sense, is a document that tries to persuade the reader to implement a proposed plan or approve a proposed project.

pool.q: What are proposals often written in response to?
pool.explain: RFPs come from government agencies, organisations or companies.
pool.evidence: Proposals are often written in response to a Request For Proposals (RFP) by a government agency, organization, or company.

pool.q: What does a progress report do?
options: Assures the reader the project is on time and on budget, or explains why not
pool.explain: Like proposals, progress reports are persuasive.
pool.evidence: progress reports assure the reader that the project is on time and on budget, or explain rationally why things might not be going according to the initial plan.

pool.q: Which special notices do instructions use to alert readers to risks?
options: Note, warning, caution and danger notices
pool.explain: They warn about ruined equipment, failed procedures or injury.
pool.evidence: For these situations, you use special notices —note, warning, caution, and danger notices.

pool.q: What are instructions, as described in the lesson?
options: Step-by-step explanations of how to assemble, operate, repair or maintain something
pool.explain: They are one of the most common uses of technical writing.
pool.evidence: One of the most common and important uses of technical writing is to provide instructions, those step-by-step explanations of how to assemble, operate, repair, or do routine maintenance on something.

pool.q: What voice and tone does the Google style guide recommend?
options: Conversational, friendly and respectful, without slang
pool.explain: Sound like a knowledgeable friend.
pool.evidence: In your documents, aim for a voice and tone that's conversational, friendly, and respectful without using slang or being overly colloquial or frivolous.

pool.q: Who should your writing sound like, according to the style guide?
options: A knowledgeable friend who understands what the reader wants to do
pool.explain: Use a casual, natural, approachable voice.
pool.evidence: Try to sound like a knowledgeable friend who understands what the developer wants to do.

pool.q: How many people have an accessibility need, according to the World Health Organization estimate quoted?
options: About 15% of the world's population, more than 1 billion people
pool.explain: Accessible writing improves the experience for everyone.
pool.evidence: The World Health Organization estimates that 15% of the world's population (more than 1 billion people) have an accessibility need.

pool.q: Which tool does the guide suggest using to test your documentation's accessibility?
pool.explain: Testing with assistive technology reveals problems.
pool.evidence: Use a screen reader to test your documentation.

pool.q: Why use descriptive headings and titles?
options: They help readers navigate the browser and the page
They hide content from search engines
They are required by law in every country
pool.explain: Unique headings make jumping between sections easier.
pool.evidence: Use descriptive headings and titles because they help a reader navigate their browser and the page.

pool.q: What is internationalization?
options: Designing a product and its documentation to minimise the localisation effort
Using as many idioms as possible
pool.explain: For example, keeping all UI strings in a separate file.
pool.evidence: Internationalization: Designing a product and its associated documentation to minimize the localization effort—for example, placing all UI strings in a separate file to simplify translation.

pool.q: What does localisation involve besides translation?
options: Adapting things like local currencies and units of measurement
pool.explain: Localisation is more than translating words.
pool.evidence: This process involves more than translation—for example, using local currencies or units of measurement.

pool.q: What should you do if a sentence's meaning is still ambiguous?
pool.explain: Clear, unambiguous language helps global readers.
pool.evidence: If the meaning is still ambiguous, try rephrasing the sentence.
